claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is initially a single-phase solid solution.
The constituent elements are homogeneously distributed in the initial state.
The initial Co-free alloy has no long-range order.
At intermediate temperatures and moderate strain rates, short-range-order fluctuations evolve in the Co-free alloy.
The evolving short-range-order fluctuations transiently interact with and pin moving dislocations.
Short-range-order-mediated dislocation pinning produces dynamic strain aging.
Dynamic pinning delays dislocation motion and increases strain hardening without significantly reducing ductility.
This dynamic strain-aging mechanism underlies the favorable strength–ductility balance of the Co-free alloy relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi tested under identical conditions, the Co-free alloy will exhibit enhanced strain hardening while maintaining ductility.
The predicted advantage will be most pronounced at approximately 400–600 K and strain rates of 10^-3 to 10^-2 s^-1.
At very low or very high temperatures, the behavioral differences between the Co-free alloy and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi will diminish.
Outside the intermediate-temperature and moderate-strain-rate regime, dynamic interactions between dislocations and short-range-order fluctuations will have less impact.
Minor compositional or processing differences may affect short-range-order evolution and its influence on dislocation pinning.
A controlled comparison should test the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi under identical temperatures and strain rates.
Failure to observe increased SRO-related dislocation pinning together with improved strain hardening in the Co-free alloy within the specified regime would falsify the hypothesis.
